I’m glad you asked, and I’m really sorry for your loss. It sounds like your wife's garden was a wonderful project, and it’s totally fine to keep things simple and manageable. Here’s a beginner-friendly, practical plan for your roses in Ohio as we head into winter and toward spring.

First, a quick mindset
- Do the gentlest, most consistent routine you can manage. Even small steps make a big difference.
- The goal this winter is to protect the roses so they come back healthy next spring, with minimal fuss.

What to do now (late fall into winter in Ohio)
1) Clean up and inspect
- Rake up and remove any fallen leaves and plant debris around the roses. This helps reduce disease next season.
- Check canes for dead or blackened wood. If a cane is dead (dry, brown, no green underneath), trim it out at the base.

2) Prune lightly
- For now, don’t do heavy pruning. Just remove obviously dead or damaged wood and any crossing branches that rub together.
- If you have very old, weak growth, you can cut it back a bit more, but keep it simple. The idea is to minimize stress on the plants.

3) Watering and feeding
- Stop feeding (fertilizing) now. Roses don’t need nutrients as the weather cools.
- Water only if the weather is dry for an extended period. If you have rain that’s enough, you don’t need to water.

4) Winter protection
- Mulch: apply a 3–6 inch layer of organic mulch (straw, shredded leaves, or wood mulch) around the base, keeping it a little away from the crown itself to avoid rot.
- Extra protection (optional but helpful in windy or exposed sites): loosely wrap the rose feet with burlap or place a simple rose cone around the plant. If you use burlap, don’t seal it tight—air needs to circulate.
- If you’re in a particularly windy or exposed spot, a bit more protection helps. If you’re not sure, start with mulch and leave the wrapping as a backup if you notice extreme cold.

What to do in early spring (when the danger of hard frost starts to fade)
1) Uncover gradually
- As temperatures rise, remove some of the mulch first to let the crown warm up, then remove the protective wrap if you used it.

2) Pruning for shape and health
- In late winter or very early spring (before new growth really starts), prune again to shape and to remove any dead or crossing wood.
- A simple approach for beginners: cut back to a strong bud on each healthy cane, remove any dead wood, and keep the center open to improve air flow. Don’t try to “hard prune” all at once if you’re unsure.

3) Fertilizing and care
- When new shoots start, you can begin a light feeding with a balanced rose fertilizer or compost tea. Follow package directions and water well.
- Water at the base of the plant, not from above, to reduce disease risk.
- Resume regular, light maintenance for a few weeks, then increase as needed.

A simple, workable routine you can follow
- Weekly (about 10–15 minutes): quick check for any damaged canes, remove any spent flowers, and keep the area free of fallen leaves.
- After rain: check soil moisture around the root zone. If it’s dry a few inches down, give a slow, deep watering.
- Every few weeks in growing season: a light fertilize or compost top-up and a mulching refresh if the mulch has settled.

Thank you for sharing that. It sounds like the garden is a meaningful bridge to your wife, and it’s wonderful you’re taking a simple, doable approach. Here’s a straightforward way to tell which roses to deadhead (remove spent blooms) and how to do it.

How to tell if a bloom is spent
- Petals are faded or falling off, and the bloom looks washed out or droopy.
- The center is starting to form a hip (the seed pod) or the bloom has obvious seed formation; the bloom isn’t going to open again.
- There’s little or no new bud development on that same stem, and you’d like the plant to direct energy to new growth.

Quick, beginner-friendly deadheading for hybrid teas
- When you notice a spent bloom, grab clean bypass pruners and put on gloves.
- Locate the nearest healthy bud or the first leaf with five leaflets on that stem.
- Cut the stem back to just above that bud or above that leaf, about 1/4 inch above the leaf node. Make a clean, angled cut so water runs off the cut.
- If the bloom is really faded and the stem is weak, you can cut a little farther back to reach a strong bud, but don’t cut too aggressively all at once.
- Remove the spent bloom cluster and any leaves that look diseased. Dispose of them (don’t compost disease-damaged material).

A few tips to keep it simple
- Do this on a regular schedule during the growing season—about every 1–2 weeks as blooms appear.
- Work from the outer edge of the bed inward so you don’t miss blooms.
- Keep tool blades clean (wipe with alcohol between plants if you’re doing several) to prevent plant disease.
- Water at the base and mulch to keep plants healthy; avoid getting leaves wet when possible.

Winter considerations for Columbus (zone 6a)
- You can continue light deadheading through spring as blooms come, then prune more significantly in late winter/very early spring.
- In late fall, keep pruning light and finish with a good mulch to protect roots over winter.
